description_full: TransDigm Group Incorporated designs, produces, and supplies aircraft components in the United States and internationally. The Power & Control segment offers mechanical/electro-mechanical actuators and controls, ignition systems and engine technology, specialized pumps and valves, power conditioning devices, specialized AC/DC electric motors and generators, batteries and chargers, databus and power controls, sensor products, switches and relay panels, hoists, winches and lifting devices, cargo loading and handling systems, delivery systems, and electronic components. Its Airframe segment provides engineered latching and locking devices, engineered rods, engineered connectors and elastomer sealing solutions, cockpit security components and systems, cockpit displays, lavatory components, seat belts and safety restraints, engineered and customized interior surfaces and related components, thermal protection and insulation products, lighting and control technology, parachutes, specialized flight, wind tunnel and jet engine testing services and equipment, and testing and instrumentation solutions, as well as engineered audio, radio, and antenna systems. The Non-Aviation segment offers seat belts and safety restraints; mechanical/electromechanical actuators and controls; hydraulic/electromechanical actuators and fuel valves; refueling systems; and turbine controls. It serves engine and power system and subsystem suppliers, airlines, third party maintenance suppliers, military buying agencies, and repair depots; airframe manufacturers, cabin system and subsystem suppliers, airlines, and third party maintenance suppliers; and off-road vehicle and subsystem suppliers, child restraint system suppliers, and satellite and space system suppliers, as well as manufacturers of heavy equipment. The company was formerly known as TD Holding Corporation and changed its name to TransDigm Group Incorporated in 2006. The company was founded in 1993 and is headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio.

financial_summary: Transdigm Group Incorporated is a large-cap industrials business with a $66.2B market cap on $8.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +18% over the past three years and +13% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 8% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 55% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.8B in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.98× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.8× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 4.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 47% operating margin runs 38pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 4.28x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 1.0% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+5.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 13% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 1.01, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $428.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 63% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 47% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $1,185 (margin of safety -1%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 60%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $708 to $1,891 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 36.3 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 18.9 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 36.4 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 6% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 20 covering analysts target $1,414 on average, 18% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 8.1% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.24).
It runs a 55% gross margin and converts 21% of revenue into free cash flow.
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.3% of revenue on R&D and 1.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.8x net debt to EBITDA ($2.8B of cash against $29.3B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.81 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
Working capital ties up about 246 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
Goodwill makes up 46% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 17.6% over 3 years, 11.6% over 5 years and 12.6% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 30% of profits supports about 5.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.4% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (2.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 30, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 98%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (170 sales, net $70.1M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.0% (0.8% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 1.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 16,500 employees, each generates about $535K of revenue, 1.5x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 17.1% a year.
That works out to $110K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $28.5M (53x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
